flashcards.q: Why can't the total runtime of subset/permutation/combination generation be optimized below O(2^n), O(n!), or O(C(n,k)) respectively?
flashcards.a: Those are the actual output sizes -- there really are that many subsets, permutations, or combinations. You cannot list a result set faster than its own size, so the only available optimization lever is pruning branches that provably can't produce a valid result.

flashcards.q: What is the three-step backtracking template underlying subset, permutation, and combination generation?
flashcards.a: Choose (add an element to the path / mark it used), explore (recurse one level deeper), un-choose (remove it from the path / unmark it used) -- always in that order, before trying the next sibling option.

flashcards.q: Why must you record a COPY of the path list at each valid result, rather than a reference to the live list?
flashcards.a: The path list continues being mutated (appended and popped) throughout the rest of the traversal. Storing a live reference means every recorded result reflects whatever the path looks like at the very end of the whole search, not what it looked like at the moment that specific result was found.

flashcards.q: For Subsets II (duplicates in input, no duplicate subsets in output), what exactly must the duplicate-skip condition compare?
flashcards.a: Skip index i (where i > start, the current branching point) if nums[i] == nums[i-1] -- comparing only SIBLINGS already tried at this exact recursion level, sorted first. It must not compare against elements from earlier recursion levels already consumed into the path.

flashcards.q: For Permutations II (duplicates in input), what is the duplicate-skip condition, and why is it subtly different from Subsets II's condition?
flashcards.a: Skip choosing nums[i] if nums[i] == nums[i-1] AND used[i-1] is False. The used[i-1]==False check is needed because permutations reconsider the ENTIRE remaining set at every level (not a forward-moving start window like combinations/subsets), so the simpler sibling-only check from Subsets II isn't sufficient here.

flashcards.q: In backtracking-based combination generation, what single character changes 'elements may be reused' (Combination Sum) into 'each element used at most once' (Combination Sum II)?
flashcards.a: The start index passed into the recursive call after choosing nums[i]: start=i allows reuse (the same element can be chosen again), start=i+1 disallows reuse (only forward, unused elements remain eligible).

flashcards.q: When should you avoid backtracking-based enumeration for a question like 'count the number of subsets summing to a target'?
flashcards.a: When only the COUNT is needed, not the actual subsets. This reduces to a knapsack-style counting DP (dp[s] = number of ways to reach sum s) in O(n * target), pseudo-polynomial time, versus exponential backtracking-with-a-counter that still visits every subset branch just to check its sum.

flashcards.q: How does Permutation Sequence (LC60) find the k-th permutation directly without generating all n! permutations?
flashcards.a: Using the factorial number system: at each position, the number of remaining permutations per choice of next digit is (remaining_count - 1)!. Divide the target index by that factorial to pick the next digit from the remaining set, reduce the index modulo that factorial, and repeat for the next position -- O(n^2) instead of O(n!).

flashcards.q: What pruning check speeds up fixed-size-k Combinations (LC77) without changing correctness?
flashcards.a: Before entering a branch, check that enough elements remain to complete the combination: len(nums) - start + 1 >= k - len(path). Without it, the algorithm still produces correct output but wastes time descending into branches that mathematically cannot reach length k.

flashcards.q: How does N-Queens-style backtracking differ in emphasis from plain subset/permutation generation, even though it uses the same choose/explore/un-choose skeleton?
flashcards.a: N-Queens layers a validity check (non-attack condition against all previously placed queens) on EVERY candidate choice before recursing deeper, requiring aggressive pruning to be tractable. Plain subset/permutation generation has no such per-choice constraint -- it's purely about enumerating the raw combinatorial structure, which is why constraint-heavy problems like N-Queens are treated as the flagship example of the separate Backtracking pattern instead.
